name: White Salmon Glacier

ways.name: White Salmon Lodge road
ways.season: spring; snow cover strongly preferred
ways.notes: Small pull-off at the old White Salmon lodge on the Mount Baker Highway. Walk around the gate and take the old road past the lodge site for about a mile until it ends at an old clearcut. With good snow, descend northeast to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up to the toe of the glacier. Without good snow, do NOT go down into the valley — hold your height entering the clearcut and contour, shedding elevation only to get around rock bands and stream crossings. This is the same decision that governs the North Face approach, and it is the difference between a walk and a fight with slide alder. Going south past Lake Ann and over Austin Pass is not the way parties reach the White Salmon Glacier; the drainage is entered from the White Salmon side of the highway.

ways.name: Mount Baker Ski Area (Chair 8) traverse
ways.season: winter/spring, on skis
ways.notes: From the base of Chair 8, traverse downhill into the bottom of the White Salmon Creek valley and then climb over four thousand feet to near the base of Hell's Highway at the top of the glacier. This is the ski-descent party's usual line in.

priorPrimaryResearch: The White Salmon lodge road is the climbers' approach, and Chair 8 is the ski-descent line. The paragraph wrongly routes over Austin Pass and Lake Ann, which variant 0's notes explicitly reject, so it describes neither.

name: Standard Scramble (Putvin Trail / Lake of the Angels approach)

ways.name: Putvin Trail to Lake of the Angels, then west to the saddle north of Point 5945
ways.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, and this peak holds avalanche-capable snow in its upper gullies later than most — slides have been reported in August and September
ways.notes: This is the standard approach to Mount Skokomish. The Putvin Trailhead (Trail #813) is on Hamma Hamma Road (FR-25), about 11.8-12.1 miles west of US-101 and about 4.5 miles past the Lena Lake trailhead, at roughly 1,600 ft. The trail is unmaintained for its last stretch but well-travelled and easy to follow when snow-free — steep, narrow, unstable footing in places through forest. Around 1.5-2 miles it breaks into the open grassy Whitehorse Creek basin, then climbs to Lake of the Angels at about 4,850-4,920 ft, roughly 3.5 miles and 3,400 ft of gain, 2-2.5 hours at a moderate pace. That is the last reliable water and the standard camp.

ways.name: Mildred Lakes Trail from Hamma Hamma Road, the west-side approach
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the off-trail brush above the lakes is much easier with lingering snow cover
ways.notes: This is not the standard approach, but it is a real approach into the Skokomish-Cruiser-Lincoln group, and it is the usual way to Mount Cruiser and Mount Lincoln. From the Mildred Lakes trailhead on Hamma Hamma Road, the trail drops into a brushy ravine to ford Huckleberry Creek at about 2,000 ft near 1.4 miles — the last reliable water before the hard part, and easy to lose in poor light. It then gains roughly 1,000 ft in about half a mile on hand-and-foot root and rock ladders, one pitch near 75-80 degrees, to a ridge high point at about 4,100 ft near 2.5 miles. From the ridge the trail drops about 250 ft to Lower Mildred Lake and continues past Middle to Upper Mildred Lake in a wooded bowl between Mount Lincoln and Mount Cruiser at about 3,850 ft near 4.3 miles, with informal camps on rock benches and the last dependable water before going off-trail. Above the lakes the route leaves the lakeshore path entirely into slide-alder and heather bushwhacking that neighbouring-peak accounts describe as very brushy, climbing to an open basin and connecting saddle beneath Skokomish's south peak at about 5,500 ft.

priorPrimaryResearch: Variant 0 notes: 'THIS IS THE STANDARD APPROACH'; variant 1 recorded only because waypoints describe it. Prose describes Putvin/Lake of the Angels.

name: Silver Glacier

ways.name: From Ross Lake by boat and up Silver Creek to the lake basin camp
ways.season: Late July through September
ways.notes: Book a water taxi for the long run up Ross Lake and get dropped at the mouth of Silver Creek at about 1,600 ft. A trail climbs the north side of the creek roughly two and a half miles to an old cabin at about 2,900 ft; above that the route is cross-country with occasional blazes, across slide alder and forest slopes, to the camp in the Silver Lake basin at about 6,763 ft. This is the shorter side for this particular route and it keeps the whole trip inside the United States, at the cost of depending on a boat.

ways.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border, over the col between the two peaks
ways.season: Late July through September, and only with passports
ways.notes: The other way in starts on the Canadian side: a rough spur off the lake road to a washout at about 2,600 ft, an overgrown roadbed to the boundary obelisk and register, and then the climbers' path up the creek through old growth to the falls, whose wet slabs and old fixed hand-line are the crux of the walk-in. Above them the path leads to the lake camp at about 5,700 ft. From that camp the way to this route climbs toward and over the col between the two peaks rather than onto the south-west side.

priorPrimaryResearch: SummitPost and most trip reports call Depot Creek from Chilliwack Lake the easiest and usual Spickard approach, and the Silver Glacier route starts at the Custer-Spickard saddle reached from Ouzel Lake; the Ross Lake boat / Silver Creek approach is less used. Paragraph gives both camps.

name: Southwest Route / Silver Lake

ways.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border to the lake camp
ways.season: Late July through September, for a crossable glacier and a passable creek
ways.notes:
From the road washout at about 2,600 ft, reached by a rough spur off the lake road on the Canadian side, walk the old roadbed about nine minutes to an inconspicuous spur on the left, follow that spur four minutes to a T-junction, and bear right onto an extremely overgrown and sporadically muddy road for about thirty-five minutes. That brings you to the boundary obelisk, where there is a register - carry a passport, because this approach crosses the international border on foot.

Above the boundary the way becomes a crude but discernible climbers' path along the creek through old growth, easy where deadfall has been cut and full of uncut logs where it has not. About three miles in it reaches the falls, which are the real crux of the approach: wet slick boulders and slabs at their base, with steep steps rigged with an old fixed hand-line. Treat the line as an aid rather than as protection, and back it up with a heavy pack on.

Above the falls the path continues through meadow and upper valley to the lake at roughly 5,700 ft - flat sandy mostly treeless benches at the toe of the talus, the standard base camp for this peak and its neighbour, with reliable water.

ways.name: From Ross Lake by boat and up Silver Creek to the lake basin
ways.season: Late July through September, once the boat is running and the cross-country is clear of snow
ways.notes:
The other side of the mountain is reached without leaving the United States. A booked water taxi runs a long way up Ross Lake to a drop at the mouth of Silver Creek at about 1,600 ft. A trail climbs the north side of the creek for roughly two and a half miles to an old cabin at about 2,900 ft, above which the way is cross-country with occasional blazes across slide alder and forest slopes to the camp in the Silver Lake basin at about 6,763 ft.

This puts you on the opposite side of the peak from the Depot Creek camp, so it changes which col you reach and in what order - plan the climb from this camp rather than translating a description written from the other one.

priorPrimaryResearch: Depot Creek (from the Canadian side up to the border) is the usual Silver Lake approach; Ross Lake/Silver Creek is the much longer all-US alternative.

name: Standard Scramble (Marmot Lake / Duckabush approach)

ways.name: Duckabush River Trail to the unmarked creek turnoff
ways.season: Mid-July to September
ways.notes: Twenty-odd miles up the Duckabush over Big Hump, with a wide ford of the river above Duckabush Camp that runs thigh-deep and swift in early season. The climbers' line leaves the maintained trail roughly three miles below Marmot Lake. A multi-day backpack with a high camp at the lake or in the basin, never a car-to-car day.

ways.name: First Divide and the unnamed lake basin
ways.season: Mid-July to September
ways.notes: Parties generally find this the easier of the two lines and it is much shorter, but the corridor on that side has been closed by fire damage — confirm before planning around it. From the divide the route runs west into a basin, then over a col and north along the crest.

priorPrimaryResearch: The route is named for the Duckabush approach. First Divide (variant 1) is shorter, but the North Fork Skokomish trail is closed by Bear Gulch Fire damage between Staircase Rapids and Home Sweet Home (ONP/USFS closure notices), so Duckabush is the usable standard for now.

name: South Route via Lake of the Angels

ways.name: Putvin Trail from Hamma Hamma Road to Lake of the Angels
ways.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Snow lingers in the basin above the lake well into summer
ways.notes:
From the Putvin Trailhead on Hamma Hamma River Road (FS 25) at about 1,565-1,600 ft — an unmarked roadside pullout, roughly 4.5 miles past the Lena Lake Trailhead — the Putvin Trail is an unmaintained, primitive user trail that climbs steeply and directly from the first steps. Expect root-staircase steps and boot-track tread through forest for the first mile. In recent years a slide near road mile 10.5 has at times blocked the last 1.2 miles of road, adding a road-walk; check Forest Service status.

About halfway up the trail meets a rock headwall requiring hand-over-hand climbing, with a large tree root as the key handhold and, historically, a fixed handline on the steepest pitch. Above it the trail eases into subalpine forest and heather meadows, passing near Whitehorse Basin and the Pond of the False Prophet, and reaches Lake of the Angels at roughly 4,850-4,920 ft in a cirque below Mount Stone's south face — about 3 to 3.5 miles and 3,000 ft of gain. Little to no reliable water on the lower trail; carry enough to reach the lake.

ways.name: Lena Lake and Upper Lena Lake, the St. Peter's traverse from the east
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the off-trail benches and passes are largely clear
ways.notes:
The other side of the same notch. From the Lena Lake Trailhead on FS 25 at roughly 600-750 ft, take the well-graded Lena Lake Trail #810 about 3 miles to Lena Lake at about 1,800 ft, then the steep primitive tread up the West Fork Lena Creek drainage roughly 3.5 more miles to Upper Lena Lake at about 4,550 ft, some 6.5 miles and 4,000 ft from the trailhead. Upper Lena Lake is the last maintained-trail camp and the last reliable water before the traverse goes cross-country; wilderness permit and bear canister required.

From Upper Lena Lake, leave the trail and head west on the Scout Lake way-trail across meadows and heather past Lena Tarn to Scout Pass at about 5,200 ft, down slightly to Upper Scout Lake, round it into Scout Basin, and up to Ullin's Pass at about 5,000 ft above the tarns known as Ullin's Bathtubs. From there a rising traverse above the small lakes leads to a snow ramp across a steep hillside below Mount Stone that ends at a loose moraine, and then exposed dirt-and-mud slopes to St. Peter's Gate at about 5,950 ft.

This is a two- or three-day trip and it is chosen for the country it crosses, not because it is quicker.

priorPrimaryResearch: Route is named for Lake of the Angels; Lena Lakes/St. Peter's traverse is a 2-3 day scenic alternative per its own notes. Prose describes Putvin.

name: Cascadian Couloir

ways.name: Longs Pass from Esmeralda TH — summer scramble
ways.season: Jul-Sep, once the couloir has melted to talus
ways.notes: Drive the North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737) to the Esmeralda Basin road-end parking at about 4,243 ft. A quarter mile of old mining road leads to a fork; take the right branch for Longs Pass. The trail climbs an open, south-facing hillside with essentially no shade — in July and August this is a pre-dawn start, not a preference. Longs Pass sits around 6,200-6,250 ft, roughly 2,000 ft above the car in about two miles, and it is the single most useful place on the whole approach. From the pass, drop the steep loose scree on the north side, losing 1,200-1,400 ft to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft. Cross the creek — there is a summer log crossing, and in high melt it is worth walking to find it rather than wading — then follow the Ingalls Creek Trail upvalley (west) a short way to the meadow and camps below the couloir's outlet. Good camps sit on the valley floor more or less straight south of where the couloir comes down, with a few more near the footlog. From camp a climbers' path threads the meadow to the toe of the couloir. This is also the standard descent for the North Ridge, West Ridge and most of the rest of Stuart, so expect to share it.

ways.name: Longs Pass from Esmeralda TH — spring snow climb
ways.season: May-Jun as a snow route; road access is the limiting factor earlier
ways.notes:
The same line, in a completely different medium. With the couloir snow-filled it is a straightforward steep snow climb rather than a scree grind, and many parties prefer it this way — but it demands axe and crampons, an early start, and a hard turnaround, because the whole thing faces south and softens fast.

FR 9737 is a gravel road that is not maintained through winter and is generally not clear until late June in a heavy year, so a genuinely early-season attempt means adding road miles on foot or ski. Check the road before committing.

The Longs Pass hillside carries avalanche exposure in winter and spring conditions, and the north-side drop to Ingalls Creek holds snow that can be firm and icy at dawn and slushy by mid-morning.

priorPrimaryResearch: Summer Esmeralda/Longs Pass scramble is the standard; spring snow climb is the same line in a different season.

name: Ice Cliff Glacier

ways.name: Stuart Lake trailhead and the Mountaineer Creek valley to the 5,400 ft basin
ways.season: Roughly Apr-Jun; the ice cliff and the couloir exit get harder and more broken as the season runs on
ways.notes: Start at the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road, about 3,400 ft. Follow the main trail to the first fork, roughly two and a half to three miles in near 4,600 ft, and stay right for Stuart Lake. Left is Colchuck Lake, a different basin on the other side of the ridge. About a mile to a mile and a half past that junction, the Stuart Lake trail turns uphill and swings right, away from the water, and begins switchbacking. That turn is your cue. Leave the trail there and stay flat in the valley bottom with Mountaineer Creek. The test is simple and works in poor visibility: if you are gaining elevation on switchbacks you are walking to Stuart Lake and you have missed it. Cross Mountaineer Creek on logs. There is no single canonical log and parties describe several sporty crossings that shift with the snowpack; early season, snowbanks make dropping onto a log awkward. On the far side, pick up the climbers' path along the creek. It is unmaintained, full of blowdown and re-routes, and the cairns are not to be trusted: they invite you up and right into a boulder slope around 4,675 ft. Two parties independently say stay low beside the creek instead, with the creek on your left — the path is unpleasant but the better line. Some parties do use the boulder field deliberately to avoid the creek crossings, so treat it as a genuine choice rather than a mistake. After about a mile and a half the valley steepens. Turn right and west and climb talus and forest into a hanging flat basin at about 5,400 ft, under the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers. That right-turn-and-climb out of a steepening valley into flat ground is the arrival cue for the bivy.

ways.name: Early-season approach with the Eightmile road gated
ways.season: Spring, roughly Apr-May, when the route is in as snow and ice
ways.notes:
When Eightmile Road is snowed or gated below the trailhead, add roughly two and a half miles of road before the trail proper. Parties walk that stretch and then put skis on, skinning the Stuart Lake trail, before continuing on foot.

This is a genuinely different day rather than a longer walk: the valley is snow-covered, the log crossings may be buried or may be harder to reach off a snowbank, and the boulder-field-versus-creek question largely disappears under snow. Postholing on the cross-country section is the common complaint.

No reliable published trailhead-to-bivy time exists for either version, so plan from your own pace rather than from a number.

priorPrimaryResearch: Summer road-open approach via Stuart Lake TH/Mountaineer Creek is the normal line; variant 1 is only the spring gated-road version of the same walk.

name: North Ridge (Complete)

ways.name: North side — Stuart Lake TH via Mountaineer Creek
ways.season: Jun to mid-Jul is the sweet spot; workable through Sep
ways.notes:
Park at the Stuart Lake Trailhead at the end of FR 7601 (Eightmile Road) out of Leavenworth and walk the Stuart Lake Trail up Mountaineer Creek. At the signed split roughly two miles along, ignore the Colchuck Lake branch on the right and carry straight on. A short distance further you leave maintained tread altogether, well before Stuart Lake, ford Mountaineer Creek and follow its south fork upstream cross-country. Late in the season there is a cairned climbers' path through much of this; early in the season there is not, and the creek runs hard.

Above the streamside travel a steep, unstable talus and boulder slope lifts you into the hanging basin under Sherpa Peak and the Sherpa Glacier. This basin holds the usual bivies. From it you angle up onto the glacier bench beneath the ridge.

This is the shorter, lower-gain way in and it puts you at the toe with the most in the tank, but it commits you to a car shuttle: the standard descent is the Cascadian Couloir, which spills out on the far side of the range at Ingalls Creek. Parties report the shuttle drive between the two trailheads costing several hours round trip. In June and early July the Sherpa Glacier is a reasonable way back down to this side and removes the shuttle problem — later in the summer it is not.

There is running snowmelt near the toe of the ridge (reported around 47.48095, -120.89454); above the 8,200 ft notch there is no reliable water once the last snow patch there melts out.

ways.name: South side — Esmeralda TH over Longs Pass and Goat Pass
ways.season: Jul-Sep, once the traverse under the Stuart Glacier has melted or consolidated
ways.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737), take the trail over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek to Goat Pass, then traverse east beneath the Stuart Glacier, staying above the large moraine mound, and aim for the toe of the ridge.

About 2,000 ft of the day is descent, so the round trip is more work than the raw gain suggests, and parties consistently report it taking longer than planned — budget eight hours and expect route-finding on the traverse rather than tread.

The reason to accept the longer, higher approach is that it removes the shuttle entirely. The Cascadian Couloir descent drops to Ingalls Creek on this side, so a party that walked in from Esmeralda walks out to its own car. Parties who came in from the north do not.

How much snow remains on the Goat Pass traverse is the recurring gear question here: sections have been reported at around 40 degrees, and whether you need an axe and traction changes week to week through the summer. Recent photos and current reports are worth more than any fixed answer.

priorPrimaryResearch: The north side from the Stuart Lake trailhead via Mountaineer Creek is the standard North Ridge approach, and Esmeralda over Longs and Goat Pass is the longer alternative.

name: South Ridge

ways.name: Boston Basin, rising traverse to the Taboo Glacier
ways.season: Jun-Sep
ways.notes:
From the unsigned Boston Basin pullout on Cascade River Road at roughly 3,300 ft (about 21.7 miles from Marblemount, directly opposite Johannesburg), take the old Diamond Mine roadbed about three quarters of a mile to a mile, then the sharp right turn onto the steep climbers' trail. Four small creek crossings, treeline about 5,300 ft, low camp 5,300-5,500 ft, high camp about 6,200-6,400 ft.

From high camp leave any semblance of trail and make a rising traverse to the northwest, holding roughly the 6,200 ft contour across talus, tundra and slab steps. You pass beneath the south spur of Forbidden Peak and cross a prominent rock rib below the cliffs, with the Taboo Glacier coming into view above.

Gain the Taboo Glacier on its climber's-left side and follow it up. Some parties skip the summit-day traverse entirely by carrying up the Taboo and camping at about 7,100 ft directly beneath Torment's southeast face at the foot of the couloir.

This traverse is the part that gets people lost in cloud. It is open, uniform ground with no trail, and in early season the creek channels are buried and there is avalanche exposure across it.

ways.name: Torment Basin climbers' path
ways.season: midsummer once brush is passable
ways.notes:
A separate and much less-used way in that skips Boston Basin altogether. Drive Cascade River Road only about 20 miles — roughly a mile past the Eldorado Creek trailhead — and look for the climbers' path starting about fifty feet upstream of the bridge over the Cascade River.

It is a steep, hard climb on a boot path that is mostly easy to follow up into Torment Basin, but despite decades of traffic some sections stay genuinely brushy. It puts you on the west side of the South Ridge rather than the east.

The reason to use it is the moat: from the Torment Basin side the South Ridge can be gained at about 6,600 ft without crossing the moat at the top of the Taboo Glacier, which is the late-season crux of the standard approach. It is also the shorter drive.

priorPrimaryResearch: Variant 1 notes call Torment Basin 'much less-used'; Boston Basin/Taboo Glacier is the standard and is what the prose describes.

ways.name: Mount Townsend Trail #839 from the Upper Trailhead
ways.season: Late June to October
ways.notes: Three sets of switchbacks, the last fully sun-exposed and the hottest, most water-hungry part of the day — there is no dependable creek on the trail itself. Camp Windy and an unmarked spur to Windy Lake sit at about 5,300 ft. The Lower Trailhead adds roughly two round-trip miles and five hundred feet. The small upper lot fills early on summer weekends.

ways.name: Little Quilcene Trail over Little River Summit
ways.notes: The shortest way to the top, with the least gain. The trail climbs steadily through forest to Little River Summit, then follows an open, exposed ridge for the last mile to meet the main trail near the summit. Carry water, as the ridge is dry and sunny.

name: Standard Scramble (above Lake Cushman)

ways.name: FR-2419 up the Big Creek drainage to the road-end trailhead
ways.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, best Jul-Sep. Spring and early summer put avalanche-capable snow in the gully
ways.notes:
From the T-intersection at the end of North Lake Cushman Road, go right onto FS Road 24 for about 1.5 miles, then left onto FS Road 2419 and follow it up the Big Creek drainage roughly 6.6 miles to its end at a small trailhead at about 3,026 ft. Northwest Forest Pass to park; no wilderness permit is needed.

From here the trail quickly becomes a boot path and then largely off-trail scrambling — there is no numbered maintained trail for most of the route. It climbs directly and steeply through forest, hand-over-hand on roots and rock in places, to a couple of open meadow benches around 3,800 ft. That meadow band holds the most reliable early-season water via snowmelt seeps; by mid-to-late summer expect it dry, so carry what you need from the car.

ways.name: From Mount Ellinor, across the connecting ridge or the west-side basin
ways.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
ways.notes: Recorded as an approach because parties do reach Washington from Ellinor rather than from Big Creek, usually as half of a traverse. Ellinor is reached by Trail #812 from its Upper or Lower Trailhead, both on the same North Lake Cushman Road corridor, and from Ellinor's summit the connecting ridge runs northeast toward Washington. It is not a walk. The crest is fractured, weathered pillow basalt with sustained Class 4 scrambling past a series of gendarmes, and it carries a loose 50 ft downclimb that most parties call the least enjoyable part of the day. The alternative that several parties prefer is the west-side basin traverse: drop into the basin below the crest and cross it, rejoining Ellinor's standard winter route line rather than fighting the ridge. Used as an approach to Washington this is a long way round for a peak with a 3.2 km trail of its own, and it is here for traverse parties.

priorPrimaryResearch: Paragraph is the FR 2419 Big Creek road-end approach (v0); v1 from Ellinor is for traverse parties.
